certification.description: Voluntary Code of Practice. Since IS 10290:1982 is an engineering guideline and operational code of practice for geological exploration and photogeological mapping rather than a direct consumer product, it does not carry an individual mandatory BIS 'ISI Mark' product stamp. However, compliance with its recommended photograph scales, contour ranges, operational flow sequences, and site suitability guidelines is strictly mandated by the Central Water Commission (CWC), Geological Survey of India (GSI), and state water resources departments when preparing Detailed Project Reports (DPRs), tender packages, and environmental clearances for dam, tunnel, and powerhouse sites across India. Precious metal hallmarking is completely inapplicable.
requirements:
Specifies three mandatory physical assets required to construct an interpreted photogeological map:
a) High-quality aerial photographs;
b) A stereoscope; and
c) Topographic base maps with contours.
The photo-interpreted map represents a preliminary stage and MUST be field checked and verified on-ground to correct interpretations, add on-site details, and prepare the final geological profiles.

Specifies contour intervals matching the selected photographic and mapping scale, ranging from fine details of 1 m to 5 m (for 1 : 5 000 scale maps) up to 5 m to 20 m (for 1 : 25 000 scale feasibility maps) to ensure adequate vertical and topographic relief resolution.

Identifies that damage to civil structures is maximum under two geologically mapped conditions:
a) Siting structures astride or too close to a tectonic feature (such as active faults, shear zones, or joints) activated during an earthquake; or
b) Siting structures on deep alluvial deposits or unconsolidated materials (which suffer far more severe damage than bedrock during seismic events). Structures must be strategically moved to bedrock or safer strata as mapped.

Powerhouse site photogeological mapping requires the same comprehensive steps as a dam site, but must additionally study aerial photographs for slope stability and mapping the orientation of joints within the local rock mass.

Tunnel alignments require careful planning to avoid difficult and hazardous geological conditions. Photogeological interpretation is established as an essential tool to compare DESIGN and COST of tunnel excavation across several considered routes.

certification.description: Voluntary Code of Practice. Since IS 10447:2026 is an operational and management guideline standard rather than a physical consumer product, it does not carry an individual mandatory BIS 'ISI Mark' product certification stamp. However, compliance with its structured waste segregation, recycling limits, and slag-utilization criteria is legally audited by the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) and State Pollution Control Boards (SPCBs) under national Solid Waste Management Rules, 2016, and Hazardous Waste Rules. It is a mandatory component of Environmental Impact Assessments (EIAs) and Consent to Operate (CTO) approvals for metallurgical facilities across India.
requirements: Requires steel plants to establish comprehensive mapping and monthly tracking of solid wastes. Technical profiles are typically structured around a nominal baseline of a 2 Million Tonne Crude Steel per annum plant capacity to trace generation rates.

Mill scale must be segregated by size and reutilized directly in-plant: fine mill scale (-10 mm) is routed as direct feed to the sinter plant, medium-size scale (+6 mm) is recycled through open hearth furnaces or pelletizing mixes (up to 5 percent to increase compressive pellet strength), and coarse scale (+10 mm) is reutilized as blast furnace feed.

LD/BOF steelmaking slag (typically generated at 120 kg to 220 kg per tonne of crude steel) can be reutilized as a source of flux in the blast furnace or sinter base-mix. However, the standard specifies a strict maximum recycling limit of 30 kg to 35 kg of BOF slag per tonne of sinter mix, as high phosphorus and sulfur contents in the slag can affect metallurgical quality if exceeded.

Due to its high calcium oxide (CaO = 30 to 52 percent) and magnesium oxide (MgO = 6 to 15 percent) content, BOF slag is approved for use as a soil conditioner to neutralize highly acidic agricultural soils.
Granulated blast furnace slag must be recovered and utilized to the maximum extent possible as a pozzolanic raw material for manufacturing Portland Slag Cement (PSC) to divert waste from slag dumps.

Air-cooled blast furnace slag is approved for physical infrastructure reuse, including road construction aggregates, railway ballast, or as a raw feed to manufacture insulating slag wool in accordance with IS 3677.

Coke breeze (screened out below 10 mm) and coal dust fines must be captured and reutilized as alternative fuels in sintering strands or pulverized coal injection (PCI) boilers to maximize thermal recovery.

Heavy-metal-bearing flue dust and gas-cleaning sludge containing volatile zinc, lead, or alkali compounds must be treated to recover metals, recycled under restricted ratios, or safely encapsulated and disposed of in secure landfills (SLFs) lined with geomembranes to prevent leaching.

Specifies that sulphur introduced through fuels fed to preheater kilns will not lead to significant SO2 emissions because of the strong alkaline environment inside the sintering zone, the calcination zone, and the lower stage of the preheater, ensuring this sulphur is safely captured and locked in the clinker.

Mandates maintaining an excess oxygen level of 1 percent to 3 percent O2 in the kiln flue gases. This concentration is critical to ensure satisfactory clinker and cement product quality while minimizing incomplete combustion products like carbon monoxide (CO).

Specifies that cement plants utilizing co-processing (feeding hazardous or non-hazardous wastes into cement kilns for energy and material recovery) must strictly satisfy and comply with the emission norms notified by MoEF&CC vide notification G.S.R. 497 (E).
Specifies that standard cement plants must satisfy and comply with the emission norms notified by MoEF&CC vide notification G.S.R. 496 (E).

certification.description: Voluntary Code of Practice. Since IS 12094:2018 is an engineering guideline for civil works, it does not carry an individual mandatory BIS 'ISI Mark' product stamp. However, compliance with its dimensional parameters (such as top width, freeboard, slopes, turning platforms) and analytical requirements (such as backwater analysis and HGL cover) is strictly mandated in public works department (PWD) tenders, irrigation department contracts, and flood-control project approvals by state and central agencies (including the Central Water Commission) to ensure structural safety against catastrophic breaches.
requirements: Requires determining the design HFL utilizing short-term or long-term sub-zone plans from the CWC Directorate of Hydrology, or by referencing the Rashtriya Barh Ayog Report (1980).

In the case of embankments constructed on both sides of a river, the rise in water level due to jacketing must be kept in view. A backwater analysis must be carried out to determine the afflux due to the loss in flood storage after construction.
For homogeneous embankments, a standard top width of 5.0 m to 5.5 m must be provided to accommodate maintenance and service vehicle operations.
Requires providing a structural freeboard of 1.5 m or 1.8 m above the design HFL to prevent overtopping by wave action or hydraulic surges.
Side slopes on both the river side and country side must not be steeper than 1:2 or 1:3. Slopes must be protected with turf (vegetative grass cover) to prevent erosion.

The HGL through the levee is assumed at a slope of 1:4, 1:5, or 1:6. To prevent piping and seepage failures, the countryside slope must cover the HGL by a minimum of 0.6 m of compacted soil. A 1.5 m wide berm (or wider) must be provided on the country side if required to encapsulate the HGL.
Before placing embankment soil, the base seat must be stripped of organic topsoil, roots, and loose material to an average depth of 0.3 m.
A turning platform of 3 m width and 15 m to 30 m in length must be provided at every kilometre along the levee top to facilitate safe turning and passage of maintenance vehicles.
To provide communication from one side of the embankment to the other, ramps at suitable places must be provided as per requirement to prevent subsequent unauthorized cutting of the levee slope.
Embankment design and compaction must prevent common breach modes: overtopping by floods higher than design limits, and improper soil compaction/settlement.

certification.description: Voluntary Procedural Guidelines Standard. Compliance with IS 12662 (Part 2) is verified through municipal audits, state-level urban development departments, Swachh Bharat Mission (SBM) clean city star ratings, and state pollution control boards. While there is no direct BIS 'ISI Mark' stamp for IS 12662 itself, compliance with its daily, weekly, monthly, and chemical disinfection schedules is universally mandated in public municipal collection and transport tenders across India. Precious metal hallmarking is completely inapplicable.
requirements: Requires daily inspection of all critical vehicle systems before starting collection routes. This includes engine fluids, coolant levels, tyre pressures, brake systems, steering gear, and a thorough visual check of all hydraulic hoses, hose couplings, and valves for leaks.

To prevent vector breeding (flies, mosquitoes), severe foul odours, and the buildup of highly corrosive organic municipal solid waste, the entire vehicle body—particularly the collection hopper, compaction chamber, and chassis underside—must be washed daily with high-pressure water jets.

Following high-pressure washing, the vehicle's waste containment compartments must be disinfected daily using approved disinfectants and germicides (such as sodium hypochlorite, phenol, bleaching powder, or quaternary ammonium compounds) to safeguard public health and protect conservancy workers.

Requires weekly inspection of leachate collection tanks, seals, and drainage valves. Valves must be flushed, and tanks emptied at designated disposal points. Because municipal organic waste leachate is highly acidic (typically pH 4.0 to 6.0), any bare steel or peeling paint must be cleaned immediately and treated with protective anti-corrosion, rust-preventive paint coatings.

All moving joints, bin-lifter hinges, hydraulic cylinder pivot pins, tailgate locking linkages, and sliding guide tracks must be greased weekly to prevent mechanical wear, friction buildup, and premature component seizing.

Checks of hydraulic oil levels, oil quality, suction filters, pressure relief valve settings (via standard pressure gauges), and hydraulic pump mounting bolts must be performed monthly to ensure consistent compaction forces and prevent sudden high-pressure hose bursts.

Safety equipment must be checked. Rear loading hoppers, heavy tailgates, dumper derrick arms, and container pins must feature functional mechanical safety locks/pins. Audible reversing alarms, beacon lights, reflective safety tape, and cabin warning flashers must be tested daily.

Maintenance files must demonstrate that all conservancy and workshop staff are provided with and wear proper Personal Protective Equipment (heavy-duty rubber gloves, safety goggles, face shields, protective aprons, safety boots, and masks) during cleaning, lubrication, or mechanical repairs.

Mandates that a permanent daily maintenance logbook be maintained inside the driver's cabin or workshop tracking fuel consumption, dynamic compaction cycles, lubrication dates, hydraulic filter changes, and part replacement histories.

requirements: Divide walls must be provided to separate bays having different energy dissipation arrangements (or different parameters/levels), or to allow for unsymmetrical operation of spillway gates to minimize cross-return flows, eddies, and erosion, as well as to isolate powerhouse bays or silt excluders.

For flip buckets, hydrostatic loads must also incorporate centrifugal forces in addition to the depth of water, combined with corresponding full uplift on the wall base.

Under the non-discharging condition, divide walls must be designed for hydrostatic water pressure up to the minimum tailwater level on one side, combined with full uplift, active backfill pressures, or empty conditions on the other.

Requires masonry/concrete gravity walls where the strata above the foundation at the end or sides of the spillway consists of earth or poor rock. For sound, steep rock foundations, cantilever walls or thin concrete linings anchored to rock by steel dowels or rock bolts may be utilized.
Mandates integrating a comprehensive drainage system behind the walls (utilizing filters and drainage holes) in accordance with IS 11772 to relieve hydrostatic pressures and prevent piping failures.

The design of anchorages and reinforcement must satisfy the allowable stress limits specified in IS 456 (concrete) and the detailing provisions of SP 55 to prevent pull-out or failure of the wall base under peak lateral and uplift forces.

Enforces checking the structural stability of the walls against sliding (on soil/rock interfaces) and overturning, ensuring factors of safety comply with standard limits under both normal and unusual/seismic conditions.

certification.description: Voluntary Code of Practice. Since IS 13083 is an engineering design and field installation standard rather than a retail consumer product, it does not carry an individual mandatory BIS 'ISI Mark' product certification stamp. However, compliance with its structural dimensions, cross-slopes, and pressure-tapping positions is strictly mandated in public sector tenders for irrigation channels, river gauging stations, and hydrometric networks (issued by the Central Water Commission, state water resources departments, and municipal water authorities) across India to ensure discharge measurement precision and prevent data disputes.
requirements: The standard Flat-V weir structure must have a triangular profile in the direction of flow, featuring an upstream slope of 1 (vertical) : 2 (horizontal) and a downstream slope of 1 (vertical) : 5 (horizontal) to ensure stable flow separation and high modular limits.

The cross-slope of the crest line shall lie in the range of 0 to 1:10 (shall not be steeper than 1:10). At the limit when the cross-slope is zero, the weir becomes a two-dimensional triangular profile weir.

The upstream head measurement tapping (gauge location) must be positioned at a standard distance of 10H' (where H' is the depth of the V) or as specified to ensure it is outside the local drawdown region.

Provides high modular limits typically ranging from 65 percent to 75 percent. The weir can operate accurately without drowned-flow reduction adjustments even when the downstream tailwater level submerges up to 75 percent of the upstream head.

The weir crest must be kept clean, sharp, and free from clinging debris. If the mean effective radius of the crest exceeds critical limits, refurbishment is required to prevent significant measurement errors at low flows.
The Flat-V weir is approved for gauging purposes in the non-modular (drowned) flow range, provided a pressure-recording tapping is physically incorporated directly at the weir crest.

Any observed or calculated analysis value (including discharge rates, velocity heads, and water stages) used to determine compliance must be mathematically rounded off in accordance with IS 2 : 1960. The number of significant places retained must match the standard's specified value.

requirements: Formally defines the intensity of irrigation as the percentage of the culturable commanded area (CCA) proposed to be irrigated in a given period of time, such as a crop season or a full water year.

For intensive irrigation systems (where water availability is not a limiting factor), the intensity of irrigation may be set to 100 percent or even more. This objective is met by putting the same land under multiple cropping cycles once or twice a year under different crops.

For protective irrigation systems (where water is scarce), the primary objective is to extend irrigation facilities to a larger, more dispersed area. Consequently, the design intensity is set low to distribute benefits across the community, provided the lower limit is fixed to maintain the basic viability of small agricultural landholdings.

Fixing high intensities in water-sufficient zones is shown to support better utilization of agricultural inputs (like fertilizers and modern implements) and take advantage of residual soil moisture from previous crops.

Fixing a suitable intensity requires careful evaluation of several factors, with water availability serving as the primary physical constraint. Where water is abundant, high intensities are called for, while water-scarce zones must adopt protective, lower-intensity limits.

To ensure EPE reliability, monitoring and measurement devices must be calibrated or verified regularly, with all records documented and maintained for audit verification.

Establishes guidelines to share evaluation results both internally (to management and personnel to foster awareness) and externally (via corporate sustainability and ESG reports) to demonstrate policy compliance.

requirements: Horticultural and wet biodegradable wastes must be strictly segregated at the source. Due to the high moisture content of wet organic scrap (typically exceeding 60 percent), the standard mandates pre-treatment (such as mechanical pressing, shredding, solar or low-temperature drying, and blending) to raise the raw calorific values and guarantee stable thermochemical processing.

When direct incineration or combustion is applied to dry horticultural waste or blended fuel pellets, the primary furnace combustion chamber must maintain a minimum operating temperature of 850°C with an excess oxygen level of 1 percent to 3 percent to prevent incomplete combustion, reduce carbon monoxide (CO), and minimize volatile organic compounds (VOCs).

Requires that the pyrolysis of dry horticultural woody biomass (tree prunings, dry leaves, trimmings) be conducted in the complete or near-complete absence of oxygen at temperatures between 400°C and 700°C. The process parameters must be optimized based on the desired output (solid bio-char, bio-oil, or syngas).

Specifies guidelines for partial oxidation gasification utilizing restricted air or oxygen supply to generate high-quality synthesis gas (syngas). Gasifier draft pressures and bed temperatures must be continuously monitored to prevent tar condensation in piping networks.

Specifies hydrothermal carbonization as an advanced thermochemical pathway highly suitable for highly saturated wet organic wastes. Wet biomass is processed in subcritical liquid water under elevated pressures (typically 1.0 to 2.5 MPa) and temperatures (180°C to 250°C), converting organic solids into energy-dense hydro-char without requiring energy-intensive pre-drying.

Provides guidelines to pelletize and feed dried horticultural waste into cement kilns for energy and material co-processing, provided it satisfies the strict emission limits and environmental guidelines of MoEF&CC and IS 12002.

Flue gases generated from incinerators, gasifiers, or boilers must pass through designated secondary air pollution control devices (such as cyclones, baghouses, and wet scrubbers) to ensure particulate matter, sulfur dioxide (SO2), nitrogen oxides (NOx), and acid gases are safely abated below national CPCB statutory limits.

Fly ash, bottom ash, and produced char or bio-char must be audited for heavy metal concentrations (such as lead, cadmium, mercury, and chromium) before being cleared for agricultural soil amendment or land applications, in accordance with Solid Waste Management guidelines.

Scoring of each indicator must involve three or more experts/assessors making decisions on a consensus basis. certification.description: Voluntary Procedural and Guidelines Standard. Although IS 8073:2026 is an engineering code of practice and operational guideline rather than a direct consumer product carrying an individual mandatory BIS 'ISI Mark' product stamp, its structural requirements, segregation strategies, chemical neutralizing schemes, and biological treatments are legally enforced across India by the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) and State Pollution Control Boards (SPCBs). Compliance is mandatory to secure and maintain a steel plant's statutory Consent to Operate (CTO) and Consent to Establish (CTE). Precious metal hallmarking is completely inapplicable.
requirements: Because treating all waste streams to a quality suitable for in-plant recirculation is economically unviable, plants must strictly segregate cooling water streams and less contaminated wastes from highly contaminated process wastes.

In all treatment cases, the potential for effluents to cause chemical corrosion of steel plant metals and concrete structures must be eliminated through active treatments, including super-phosphate (phosphatization) and lime (alkalization).

Wastewater from blast furnace gas cleaning and cooling must be treated by plain sedimentation in horizontal-flow sedimentation tanks (without coagulants) to reduce suspended solids (SS) to standard limits (e.g., 10 mg/l).

Spent pickle liquor from acid pickling lines must be chemically regenerated or neutralized with lime. Adding lime and air under controlled temperature and aeration conditions oxidizes ferrous hydroxide into rapidly settling and insoluble ferric hydroxide. Acid and copperas (ferrous sulphate heptahydrate) must be recovered from pickle liquor to the maximum extent economically possible.
Acid sludge generated from by-product plants is classified as hazardous waste and must be safely disposed of in a Secured Land Fill (SLF).
Caustic wash waste generated from by-product plants must be disposed of via incineration.
Brine wastewater from ion exchange resin regeneration must either be chemically reclaimed or discharged via highly controlled release to wastewater streams.
Spent cleaners utilized in surface treatment and degreasing must be segregated for oil breakout or incineration.

Coke oven wastes are rich in nitrogen but relatively low in phosphorus. Because phosphorus is required to the extent of approximately 1 percent of the Biochemical Oxygen Demand (BOD) for microbial growth, phosphorus must be supplemented during biological coke oven waste treatment.

Phenolic substances in coke oven waste demand high levels of dissolved oxygen (2 mg to 25 mg of oxygen per milligram of phenol). Biological systems must maintain adequate oxygen supplies, and plants must provide dedicated handling facilities for the substantial quantities of excess sludge generated.

Settled scale from rolling mill wastewater must be dredged from scale pits using buckets or drag-out conveyors. To prevent scale from passing over the weir, turbulent conditions must be minimized by shutting down the specific compartment of the scale pit being cleaned.

Slurry containing fly ash from power plants must be pumped to settling basins or low-lying dyked areas. The supernatant water can be reused or discharged, but the raw slurry must never be discharged directly into streams or freshwater lakes.

Ammonia and phenols must be recovered from coke oven waste to the maximum extent economically possible. The remaining wastewater can be treated in an extended aeration activated sludge process working on a complete mixing system.
If raw sewage or dilution water is available, coke oven waste can be diluted to a phenol concentration below 200 mg/l and treated in a trickling filter.

requirements: Requires backwashing the cation exchange unit with deionized water at a specified flow rate and temperature for a supplier-recommended duration before regenerating with the specified acid quantity/concentration. The bed is subsequently rinsed with deionized water.

Requires backwashing the anion exchange bed with deionized water at a specified flow rate. The resin must be regenerated using the designated quantity and concentration of alkali at supplier-specified flow/temperature rates, followed by a thorough deionized water rinse.

The two-bed deionization unit must be operated at the recommended flow rate. Operation must continue until ionic breakthrough is officially detected, monitored via an inbuilt or separate electrical conductivity meter.
Mixed bed deionizers are strictly categorized as polishing units. The standard mandates that they must not be used as a primary replacement for standard deionizing columns.

Specifies a four-step regeneration sequence: a) Backwashing with deionized water at a designated flow rate to allow the cation and anion resin layers to separate physically; b) Regenerating the separated resins using the column's internal distributor or in two different external columns; c) Re-mixing the cation and anion exchangers thoroughly using clean compressed air; and d) Rinsing the mixed bed with deionized water as recommended by the supplier.
Ion exchange resin beds must never be allowed to dry out. The deionization columns must be located completely away from high-temperature laboratory sources, including boilers, heaters, or furnaces.

If a deionizing column is expected to remain out of service for an extended period of time, the resin bed must be stored in an exhausted (unregenerated) condition rather than a fully regenerated condition.
All inlet, outlet, and bypass valves must be fully closed immediately at the end of any operation or regeneration process if the unit is not scheduled for immediate reuse.
Operators must ensure that all tube connectors, fittings, and attached conductivity meters are in proper working condition, with daily visual checks conducted to ensure zero liquid leakage.

Operators must strictly observe appropriate safety considerations and wear proper protective equipment when handling hazardous acid and alkali regeneration chemicals and managing their highly corrosive waste products.

Since IS 11388:2012 is an engineering guideline and design code rather than a direct consumer product, it does not carry a mandatory BIS 'ISI Mark' product stamp. However, compliance with its design loads, clear opening parameters, bar thicknesses, and vibration resonance limits is strictly mandated in public sector hydropower, water-diverting tunnels, and river valley intake tenders (under agencies such as NHPC, SJVN, THDC, NEEPCO, CWC, and state irrigation departments) across India to prevent structural failures, turbine damage, or water conductor blockages. Precious metal hallmarking is completely inapplicable.
requirements: Trash racks are typically installed at an incline from the vertical to facilitate manual or mechanical raking. A slope of 15 degrees from the vertical is commonly recommended to lower manual effort and ensure easy debris clearance.

Spacing of vertical bars must be as wide as possible to prolong cleaning intervals while preventing harmful debris from entering. Clear openings typically range from 7.5 to 15 cm for medium-size turbines, and 15 to 25 cm for larger-size turbines, or designed proportional to the runner diameter (e.g., 1/30 to 1/50 of runner diameter).
Trash rack bars must have a minimum thickness of 10 mm to 12 mm to provide sufficient resistance against structural bending, physical impacts of heavy debris, and corrosion.

To keep hydraulic head losses minimum and prevent debris from being drawn too tightly against the trash rack face, the approach velocity through the net area of the trash rack is generally restricted to 0.75 m/s to 1.5 m/s (typically kept below 1.5 m/s, or 1.0 m/s for normal flow conditions).
To prevent lateral-torsional buckling or excessive vibration without support, the maximum lateral unsupported length of any trash rack bar must not exceed 70 times the bar thickness (L/t <= 70).

To safeguard against sudden blocking, trash rack bars must be designed for a minimum differential hydraulic head of 6.0 m of water. The supporting steel members (beams and frames) must be designed for a higher differential head of 7.0 m of water, ensuring that the bars fail first before the supporting structure during severe blockage.

Trash rack bars are assumed to fail when the bending stress reaches:
σ = σ_y * (1.23 - 0.0153 * L / t)
where σ_y is the yield stress of the steel, L is the laterally unsupported length, and t is the bar thickness. For bars used to support flash boards, the safe working stress must not exceed 2/3 of this failure stress.

Horizontal intermediate support beams should not require stress reduction for lack of lateral support and are assumed to fail at yield point stress. However, calculations must include dead weights of both the beam and bars. To ensure rigidity during handling and operation, the lateral deflection of these beams under load must not exceed 1/325 of the span.

Trash racks must be checked for hydrodynamically induced vibration (vortex shedding). The ratio of the forcing frequency of vortex shedding (Fi) to the natural frequency (Fn) must satisfy:
Fi / Fn <= 0.6 for normal conditions, and must not exceed 0.65 for a short period.

The forced frequency of vortex shedding is calculated as:
Fi = St * Veff / t
where St is the Strouhal number (typically 0.18 to 0.22 based on bar profile), Veff is the effective velocity in the net area, and t is the bar thickness perpendicular to the flow.

The natural frequency of the trash rack must be calculated incorporating steel elasticity (E), moment of inertia (I), acceleration due to gravity (g), steel weight density (γs), bar thickness (t), and the virtual mass density of water (γbe).
